claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: acd-5 interacts with the Ca2+ oscillations.
claims.source: This shows that acd-5 does interact with the Ca2+ oscillations, albeit in a relatively subtle manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed changes in Ca2+ oscillation amplitude and interval in acd-5 mutants.

claims.claim: acd-5(ok2657) mutants exhibited significantly longer defecation cycle intervals.
claims.source: The cycle intervals observed correspond well with the Ca2+ imaging observations; acd-5(ok2657) exhibited significantly longer intervals and acd-5(lj122) animals showed no difference from wild-type (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: acd-5(lj122) animals showed no difference from wild-type in defecation cycle intervals.
claims.source: The cycle intervals observed correspond well with the Ca2+ imaging observations; acd-5(ok2657) exhibited significantly longer intervals and acd-5(lj122) animals showed no difference from wild-type (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Heterozygous acd-5(ok2657) animals retained the longer cycle phenotype.
claims.source: Heterozygous animals and wild-type animals overexpressing the acd-5(ok2657) mutant gene, under the endogenous promoter or under another intestinal promoter (Pges-1) all retained the longer cycle phenotype, supporting this hypothesis (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Wild-type animals overexpressing the acd-5(ok2657) mutant gene retained the longer cycle phenotype.
claims.source: Heterozygous animals and wild-type animals overexpressing the acd-5(ok2657) mutant gene, under the endogenous promoter or under another intestinal promoter (Pges-1) all retained the longer cycle phenotype, supporting this hypothesis (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Overexpression of the acd-5(ok2657) gene subtly increased variability.
claims.source: We also found that overexpression of the acd-5(ok2657) gene subtly increased variability, although since this was also true of overexpression of the wild-type acd-5 gene (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B), it may have been a consequence of overexpression rather than the acd-5(ok2657) mutation itself.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B.

claims.claim: Overexpression of the wild-type acd-5 gene also increased variability.
claims.source: We also found that overexpression of the acd-5(ok2657) gene subtly increased variability, although since this was also true of overexpression of the wild-type acd-5 gene (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B), it may have been a consequence of overexpression rather than the acd-5(ok2657) mutation itself.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B.

claims.claim: The IP3 receptor ITR-1 plays a critical role in the Ca2+ oscillations that drive the DMP.
claims.source: The IP3 receptor, ITR-1, plays a critical role in the Ca2+ oscillations that drive the DMP and the loss-of-function allele itr-1(sa73) results in a dramatic increase in both cycle length and variability (Dal Santo et al., 1999; Walker et al., 2002; Espelt et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The loss-of-function allele itr-1(sa73) results in a dramatic increase in both cycle length and variability.
claims.source: The IP3 receptor, ITR-1, plays a critical role in the Ca2+ oscillations that drive the DMP and the loss-of-function allele itr-1(sa73) results in a dramatic increase in both cycle length and variability (Dal Santo et al., 1999; Walker et al., 2002; Espelt et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by data in Figure 3D and E.

claims.claim: A compensatory effect is observed in itr-1(sa73) mutants where an aberrantly long cycle is followed by a short one, and vice versa.
claims.source: We observed the previously described compensatory effect (Kwan et al., 2008) in itr-1(sa73), where an aberrantly long cycle is followed by a short one, and vice versa (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: acd-5 alleles did not significantly reduce the cycle length or variability of itr-1(sa73).
claims.source: Although the acd-5 alleles did not significantly reduce the cycle length or variability of itr-1(sa73), and the compensatory effect remained intact, we did nevertheless observe a striking suppression of excessively long cycles, with an almost complete loss of cycles over 200 s (Figure 3D and E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 3D and E.

claims.claim: acd-5 alleles suppressed excessively long cycles in itr-1(sa73) mutants, with an almost complete loss of cycles over 200 s.
claims.source: Although the acd-5 alleles did not significantly reduce the cycle length or variability of itr-1(sa73), and the compensatory effect remained intact, we did nevertheless observe a striking suppression of excessively long cycles, with an almost complete loss of cycles over 200 s (Figure 3D and E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 3D and E.

claims.claim: The CV distribution was significantly different for both itr-1/acd-5 double mutants.
claims.source: A Kolmogorov-Smirnov comparison of the cumulative distribution showed that cycle length distribution was not significantly different, but the CV distribution was significantly different for both itr-1/acd-5 double mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claims.claim: acd-5 is responsible for the dysregulation that results in longer, more variable cycles in itr-1 mutants.
claims.source: This suggests that acd-5 is responsible for the dysregulation that results in those longer, more variable cycles, perhaps suggesting a role for ACD-5 in regulating cycle length that is otherwise presumably masked or overridden by the dominant influence of the Ca2+ oscillator.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction data between acd-5 and itr-1 mutants.

claims.claim: The Na+/H+ exchanger PBO-4 localises to the basolateral membrane of the posterior intestinal cells.
claims.source: The Na+/H+ exchanger PBO-4 localises to the basolateral membrane of the posterior intestinal cells, where it plays a central role in the release of protons into the pseudocoelom to trigger pBoc, and mutations result in missed or weak pBoc and frequently missed EMCs (Benomar et al., 2020; Beg et al., 2008; Pfeiffer et al., 2008), but the precise relationship between Ca2+ increase and PBO-4-mediated proton oscillations is unknown.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: PBO-4 plays a central role in the release of protons into the pseudocoelom to trigger pBoc.
claims.source: The Na+/H+ exchanger PBO-4 localises to the basolateral membrane of the posterior intestinal cells, where it plays a central role in the release of protons into the pseudocoelom to trigger pBoc, and mutations result in missed or weak pBoc and frequently missed EMCs (Benomar et al., 2020; Beg et al., 2008; Pfeiffer et al., 2008), but the precise relationship between Ca2+ increase and PBO-4-mediated proton oscillations is unknown.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: pbo-4 mutations result in missed or weak pBoc and frequently missed EMCs.
claims.source: The Na+/H+ exchanger PBO-4 localises to the basolateral membrane of the posterior intestinal cells, where it plays a central role in the release of protons into the pseudocoelom to trigger pBoc, and mutations result in missed or weak pBoc and frequently missed EMCs (Benomar et al., 2020; Beg et al., 2008; Pfeiffer et al., 2008), but the precise relationship between Ca2+ increase and PBO-4-mediated proton oscillations is unknown.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D-F.

claims.claim: PBO-4 also localises to the apical membrane.
claims.source: PBO-4 also localises to the apical membrane (Bender et al., 2013) but, as discussed earlier, its role there is controversial.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The pbo-4 mutation was dominant over the acd-5 mutations.
claims.source: The pbo-4 mutation was dominant over the acd-5 mutations, with acd-5/pbo-4 double mutants both displaying wild-type cycle length and variability (like the pbo-4 single), and EMC and pBoc defects similar to the pbo-4 mutant (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D-F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3D-F.

claims.claim: acd-5/pbo-4 double mutants displayed wild-type cycle length and variability.
claims.source: The pbo-4 mutation was dominant over the acd-5 mutations, with acd-5/pbo-4 double mutants both displaying wild-type cycle length and variability (like the pbo-4 single), and EMC and pBoc defects similar to the pbo-4 mutant (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D-F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: acd-5/pbo-4 double mutants showed EMC and pBoc defects similar to the pbo-4 mutant.
claims.source: The pbo-4 mutation was dominant over the acd-5 mutations, with acd-5/pbo-4 double mutants both displaying wild-type cycle length and variability (like the pbo-4 single), and EMC and pBoc defects similar to the pbo-4 mutant (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D-F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D-F.

claims.claim: pbo-4 acts genetically upstream of acd-5.
claims.source: This is consistent with pbo-4 acting genetically upstream of acd-5; however, this could reflect an apical role for PBO-4 (Figure 3G) or simply the dominance of basolateral proton release in driving downstream events.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction data, though alternative explanations are acknowledged.

claims.claim: FLR-1 was shown to localise to both apical and basolateral membranes.
claims.source: Previous research identified the expression of another DEG/ENaC channel gene, flr-1, in the intestine (Take-uchi et al., 1998), and it was shown to localise to both apical and basolateral membranes (Take-uchi et al., 1998; Kobayashi et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: flr-1 mutants show more severe disruption of the DMP than acd-5 mutants.
claims.source: flr-1 mutants show more severe disruption of the DMP than acd-5 mutants, leading us to hypothesise that there might be two distinct channels in the intestinal cell: A heteromeric or homomeric ACD-5-containing channel on the apical membrane and an FLR-1-containing channel on both membranes.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the phenotypes of flr-1 and acd-5 mutants.

claims.claim: FLR-1 expressed alone in oocytes did not produce pH-sensitive currents.
claims.source: Since FLR-1 expressed alone in oocytes did not produce pH-sensitive currents in our experiments, we hypothesised that FLR-1 could contribute to a heteromeric channel.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: acd-3 and del-5 are expressed in the intestine.
claims.source: Therefore, we used transcriptional fusions to search for additional intestinally expressed DEG/ENaCs. We found two such intestine-expressed genes, acd-3 and del-5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional reporter data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: ACD-5 and FLR-1 share the highest homology with mammalian ASIC2.
claims.source: Whereas ACD-5 and FLR-1 share the highest homology with mammalian ASIC2, ACD-3 shares the highest homology with mammalian ASIC5 and DEL-5 is more distantly related.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on sequence homology analysis, which is a standard bioinformatics approach.

claims.claim: ACD-3 shares the highest homology with mammalian ASIC5.
claims.source: Whereas ACD-5 and FLR-1 share the highest homology with mammalian ASIC2, ACD-3 shares the highest homology with mammalian ASIC5 and DEL-5 is more distantly related.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on sequence homology analysis.

claims.claim: DEL-5 is more distantly related to mammalian ASICs.
claims.source: Whereas ACD-5 and FLR-1 share the highest homology with mammalian ASIC2, ACD-3 shares the highest homology with mammalian ASIC5 and DEL-5 is more distantly related.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on sequence homology analysis.

claims.claim: mKate::DEL-5 and ACD-3::mKate2 showed evidence of basolateral localisation.
claims.source: We investigated the subcellular localisation of ACD-3 and DEL-5 using translational fusions. In common with FLR-1::GFP (Take-uchi et al., 1998), mKate::DEL-5 and ACD-3::mKate2, where detectable, showed a diffuse distribution. Where expression levels were more variable, we were able to observe evidence of basolateral localisation, but we cannot exclude that DEL-5 and ACD-3 are also apically localised, since this could potentially be masked (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Co-expression of FLR-1 with either DEL-5, ACD-3, or both resulted in a response to changes in pH from a holding pH 5.
claims.source: However, when we co-expressed FLR-1 with either DEL-5, ACD-3, or both, we observed a response to changes in pH from a holding pH 5 (pH50 of 6.42), a profile resembling that previously reported for the TadNaCs, DEG/ENaC channels of the marine placozoa Trichoplax adhaerens (Elkhatib et al., 2019; Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 4A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claims.claim: The FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 heteromeric channel has a pH50 of 6.42.
claims.source: However, when we co-expressed FLR-1 with either DEL-5, ACD-3, or both, we observed a response to changes in pH from a holding pH 5 (pH50 of 6.42), a profile resembling that previously reported for the TadNaCs, DEG/ENaC channels of the marine placozoa Trichoplax adhaerens (Elkhatib et al., 2019; Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 4A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: No currents were detected in response to pH when expressing DEL-5 together with ACD-3.
claims.source: We could not detect any currents in response to pH when expressing DEL-5 together with ACD-3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4C.

claims.claim: The pH50s did not change when FLR-1 (ACD-3 or DEL-5) was co-expressed with ACD-5 compared to the expression of ACD-5 alone.
claims.source: As FLR-1 has previously been proposed to localise at both the basolateral and luminal intestinal membrane (Take-uchi et al., 1998; Kobayashi et al., 2011), where it might form heteromers with ACD-5, we also co-expressed FLR-1 (ACD-3 or DEL-5) with ACD-5 in oocytes. The pH50s did not change compared to the expression of ACD-5 alone (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A,B,).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: The other subunits do not influence ACD-5 channel function.
claims.source: Co-expression can be difficult to interpret, due to the potential presence of a mix of homo-and heteromeric channels, which can confound whole-cell recordings (Hesselager et al., 2004). However, our results suggest that the other subunits do not influence ACD-5 channel function.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-expression data, though the authors acknowledge the limitations of this approach.

claims.claim: The heteromeric FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 channel is insensitive to amiloride.
claims.source: We also tested amiloride sensitivity of this heteromeric channel and found that it is insensitive to the blocker (Figure 4E), a phenomenon previously reported for a mutant DEGT-1 channel (Fechner et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4E and a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The heteromeric FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 channel did not show a significant shift in ΔErev between the monovalent cations.
claims.source: We next investigated ion selectivity, the heteromeric FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 channel did not show a significant shift in ΔErev between the monovalent cations, however, it showed a negative shift in ΔErev when switching to a CaCl2 solution with some current remaining (Figure 4F–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ion substitution data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claims.claim: The heteromeric FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 channel showed a negative shift in ΔErev when switching to a CaCl2 solution with some current remaining.
claims.source: We next investigated ion selectivity, the heteromeric FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 channel did not show a significant shift in ΔErev between the monovalent cations, however, it showed a negative shift in ΔErev when switching to a CaCl2 solution with some current remaining (Figure 4F–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ion substitution data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claims.claim: The heteromeric FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 channel is marginally permeable for Ca2+.
claims.source: This suggests that the channel is also marginally permeable for Ca2+.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of a negative shift in ΔErev with CaCl2 and some remaining current.

claims.claim: Removal of Na+ (by substituting with NMDG) induced a negative shift in ΔErev for the FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 channel.
claims.source: Removal of Na+ (by substituting with NMDG) also induced a negative shift in ΔErev (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ion substitution data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: FLR-1, together with ACD-3 and/or DEL-5, forms a functional amiloride-insensitive acid-inhibited channel with different properties to ACD-5.
claims.source: Thus, FLR-1, together with ACD-3 and/or DEL-5, appears to form a functional amiloride-insensitive acid-inhibited channel with different properties to ACD-5.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the electrophysiological characterization of the FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 channel.

claims.claim: There is a second intestinal DEG/ENaC, an FLR-1, ACD-3, and DEL-5-containing heteromeric channel localised to the basolateral membrane.
claims.source: These findings support the hypothesis that there is a second intestinal DEG/ENaC, an FLR-1, ACD-3, and DEL-5-containing heteromeric channel localised to the basolateral membrane.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on localization and electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: flr-1(ut11) mutants show high variability of DMP cycle length, with many extremely short cycles (less than 30 s).
claims.source: flr-1(ut11) mutants show high variability of DMP cycle length, with many extremely short cycles (less than 30 s) (Katsura et al., 1994; Take-uchi et al., 1998; Kwan et al., 2008; Take-uchi et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: flr-1(syb3521) is a truncation of the N-terminus and predicted TM1 with the remaining gene being out of frame so no protein is generated.
claims.source: We created flr-1(syb3521), using CRISPR/Cas9 (Dokshin et al., 2018), truncating the N-terminus and predicted TM1 with the remaining gene being out of frame so no protein is generated (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, D.

claims.claim: flr-1(syb3521) presented with a slow-growing, caloric restriction-like phenotype.
claims.source: As previously described for flr-1(ut11) and other alleles (Katsura et al., 1994; Take-uchi et al., 1998; Kobayashi et al., 2011), syb3521 presented with a slow-growing, caloric restriction-like phenotype and were thus difficult to cross.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by observations and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: flr-1(RNAi) animals exhibited the caloric restriction phenotype.
claims.source: As expected, flr-1(RNAi) animals also exhibited the caloric restriction phenotype.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on observations of RNAi-treated animals.

claims.claim: flr-1(RNAi) and flr-1(syb3521) animals showed disruption of DMP, with a dramatic increase in variability, a mix of extremely short and long cycles, missed EMCs and missed or weak pBoc contractions.
claims.source: Like flr-1(ut11), both flr-1(RNAi) and flr-1(syb3521) animals showed disruption of DMP, with a dramatic increase in variability, a mix of extremely short and long cycles, missed EMCs and missed or weak pBoc contractions (Figure 5A–D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5A-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: acd-3/del-5 double mutants phenocopied the flr-1 deficient animals.
claims.source: Interestingly, acd-3/del-5 double mutants phenocopied the flr-1 deficient animals, showing similar defects in cycle length, EMC and pBoc defects (Figure 5A–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claims.claim: flr-1(RNAi) did not significantly alter the phenotypes of acd-3/del-5 double mutants.
claims.source: flr-1(RNAi) did not significantly alter these phenotypes, suggesting that the three genes function together and further supporting the hypothesis that these three subunits form a heteromer.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 5A-E.

claims.claim: The three genes flr-1, acd-3, and del-5 function together.
claims.source: flr-1(RNAi) did not significantly alter these phenotypes, suggesting that the three genes function together and further supporting the hypothesis that these three subunits form a heteromer.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction data.

claims.claim: Neither of the acd-3 or del-5 single mutants exhibited phenotypes similar to acd-3/del-5 double mutants.
claims.source: Neither of the acd-3 or del-5 single mutants exhibited such phenotypes, suggesting that they act redundantly.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that single mutants have no phenotype while double mutants do.

claims.claim: acd-3 and del-5 act redundantly.
claims.source: Neither of the acd-3 or del-5 single mutants exhibited such phenotypes, suggesting that they act redundantly.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic data.

claims.claim: The defects observed for acd-3/del-5 double mutants were rescued by expression of the acd-3::mKate2 or mKate2::del-5 fusions.
claims.source: The defects observed for acd-3/del-5 double mutants were rescued by expression of the acd-3::mKate2 or mKate2::del-5 fusions (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Table 1), confirming that their functionality is retained and thus that the localisation observed in Figure 4A is functionally relevant.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Table 1.

claims.claim: Both the flr-1 deficient animals and the acd-3/del-5 double mutants frequently exhibited short <17 s cycles, described as 'echos'.
claims.source: Both the flr-1 deficient animals and the acd-3/del-5 double mutants frequently exhibited short <17 s cycles, seen for unc-43(sa200) CaMK II mutants and described as 'echos', since they are often incomplete (missing EMC) (Teramoto and Iwasaki, 2006; Liu and Thomas, 1994; Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5E and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Expression of either acd-3 or del-5 under an intestine-specific promoter significantly rescues all of the defects exhibited by acd-3/del-5 double mutants.
claims.source: As Figure 5—figure supplement 3 shows, expression of either acd-3 or del-5 under an intestine-specific promoter significantly rescues all of the defects exhibited by acd-3/del-5 double mutants, supporting the idea that the intestine is the site of function.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The intestine is the site of function for acd-3 and del-5.
claims.source: As Figure 5—figure supplement 3 shows, expression of either acd-3 or del-5 under an intestine-specific promoter significantly rescues all of the defects exhibited by acd-3/del-5 double mutants, supporting the idea that the intestine is the site of function.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments.

claims.claim: flr-1 is expressed only in the intestine.
claims.source: This coincides with previous observations that flr-1 is expressed only in the intestine, and that an intestinally expressed fusion rescues the flr-1 mutant phenotype (Take-uchi et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: An intestinally expressed fusion rescues the flr-1 mutant phenotype.
claims.source: This coincides with previous observations that flr-1 is expressed only in the intestine, and that an intestinally expressed fusion rescues the flr-1 mutant phenotype (Take-uchi et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Interrupting the Ca2+ wave with heparin in parts of the intestine eliminates the aBoc and EMC following the pBoc.
claims.source: Previous research has shown that interrupting the Ca2+ wave with heparin, an IP3 receptor inhibitor, in parts of the intestine eliminates the aBoc and EMC following the pBoc, suggesting that the Ca2+ wave is upstream of these steps (Teramoto and Iwasaki, 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The Ca2+ wave is upstream of aBoc and EMC.
claims.source: Previous research has shown that interrupting the Ca2+ wave with heparin, an IP3 receptor inhibitor, in parts of the intestine eliminates the aBoc and EMC following the pBoc, suggesting that the Ca2+ wave is upstream of these steps (Teramoto and Iwasaki, 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the heparin experiment cited.

claims.claim: The acd-3/del-5 and flr-1 mutations are likely to interfere with the intestinal Ca2+ wave.
claims.source: The similarities with both the itr-1 (highly variable, long cycles), and unc-43 (echos) phenotypes suggests that the acd-3/del-5 and flr-1 mutations are likely to interfere with the intestinal Ca2+ wave.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the phenotypic similarities to itr-1 and unc-43 mutants.

claims.claim: flr-1(syb3521) completely disrupted the rhythmicity of Ca2+ oscillations.
claims.source: As Figure 6 shows, flr-1(syb3521) completely disrupted the rhythmicity of Ca2+ oscillations that we normally observe in wild-type animals (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 for additional traces).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 6 and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Both the basal and maximal Ca2+ concentrations were significantly decreased in flr-1(syb3521) mutants.
claims.source: Overall, both the basal and maximal Ca2+ concentrations were significantly decreased (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B).

results.result: ACD-5 forms a homomeric, amiloride-sensitive, pH-sensitive monovalent cation channel with maximal current at pH 6, inhibition at pH 4, preference for Li+ over Na+, and impermeability to Ca2+ and protons.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C12 are well-supported by electrophysiological data from Xenopus oocytes (Figure 1A-D and supplements). The pH50 values, amiloride IC50, and ion selectivity are directly measured and reported with appropriate sample sizes (N=5-12). The reversal potential measurements and ion substitution experiments provide strong evidence for the channel's ion selectivity properties.

results.result: The acd-5(ok2657) mutation is a dominant truncation that lacks TM2 and the C-terminus, produces no functional current alone, but reduces wild-type ACD-5 current in a dose-dependent manner when co-expressed.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C17 are supported by molecular characterization (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), electrophysiological data (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and behavioral data (Figure 3C). The dose-response relationship in co-expression experiments and the dominant phenotype in heterozygotes provide strong evidence for the dominant-negative mechanism.

results.result: ACD-5 localizes to the apical membrane of intestinal epithelial cells, where the physiological pH environment is likely pH 4-6.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 are supported by confocal microscopy showing co-localization with apical markers (Figure 1F-G, Figure 1—figure supplement 4) and by citations to previous studies establishing intestinal lumen pH range. The inference about physiological pH is reasonable given the localization and known lumen pH.

results.result: acd-5 mutants show more neutral intestinal lumen pH (reduced Kansas Red fluorescence), high incidence of missed MATs, but normal MAT interval length where detectable, indicating ACD-5 controls proton concentration but not timing of the proton wave.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C31 are supported by Kansas Red fluorescence imaging (Figure 2A-D) with appropriate sample sizes (N=9-38). The rescue experiments confirm specificity. The observation that MAT interval is unaffected while pH and MAT frequency are altered provides strong evidence for the proposed role. Statistical tests are appropriate.

results.result: acd-5 mutations subtly alter intestinal Ca2+ oscillations and defecation cycle intervals, with acd-5(ok2657) showing increased amplitude and longer intervals, while acd-5(lj122) shows reduced amplitude and slightly shorter intervals.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C38 are supported by Ca2+ imaging data (Figure 3A-B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and behavioral measurements (Figure 3C) with adequate sample sizes (N=50-75). Statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U) are appropriate. The subtle effects are consistent with the proposed model that ACD-5 influences but does not drive Ca2+ oscillations.

results.result: Heterozygous acd-5(ok2657) animals and wild-type animals overexpressing acd-5(ok2657) retain the longer cycle phenotype, supporting the dominant nature of the mutation, though overexpression of either allele increases variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The retention of the phenotype in heterozygotes and overexpression lines provides strong genetic evidence for dominance. The authors appropriately note that increased variability may be due to overexpression rather than the mutation itself.

results.result: acd-5 alleles suppress excessively long cycles (>200s) in itr-1(sa73) mutants without significantly reducing overall cycle length or variability, suggesting acd-5 is responsible for dysregulation leading to very long cycles.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C49 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 3D-E, Figure 3—figure supplement 3-4) and citations to previous studies. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test appropriately shows significant difference in CV distribution but not cycle length distribution. The genetic interaction provides insight into the relationship between acd-5 and the Ca2+ oscillator.

results.result: The pbo-4 mutation is genetically dominant over acd-5 mutations, with double mutants displaying wild-type cycle length but pbo-4-like EMC and pBoc defects, consistent with pbo-4 acting upstream of acd-5.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C57 are supported by genetic interaction data (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D-F) and citations to previous studies. The epistasis analysis is appropriate, though the authors correctly note that alternative explanations (apical role for PBO-4 or dominance of basolateral proton release) cannot be excluded.

results.result: FLR-1 localizes to both apical and basolateral membranes, shows more severe DMP disruption than acd-5 mutants, does not produce pH-sensitive currents alone in oocytes, and two additional intestinally expressed DEG/ENaCs (acd-3 and del-5) were identified.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C64 are supported by citations to previous studies (C58), phenotypic comparisons (C59), electrophysiological data (C60, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), transcriptional reporter data (C61, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and sequence homology analysis (C62-C64). The evidence converges to support the hypothesis of a heteromeric channel.

results.result: ACD-3 and DEL-5 show evidence of basolateral localization; co-expression of FLR-1 with ACD-3 and/or DEL-5 produces pH-sensitive currents (pH50=6.42), while DEL-5+ACD-3 or FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5+ACD-5 do not alter ACD-5 pH50.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 are supported by confocal microscopy (Figure 4A-B) and electrophysiological data (Figure 4C-D, Figure 4—figure supplement 4-5). The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations of co-expression experiments and the possibility of mixed channel populations. The lack of effect on ACD-5 pH50 when co-expressed with other subunits supports distinct channel complexes.

results.result: The FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 heteromeric channel is amiloride-insensitive, shows no significant shift in ΔErev between monovalent cations, but shows a negative shift with CaCl2 (suggesting marginal Ca2+ permeability) and with NMDG, forming a functional acid-inhibited channel distinct from ACD-5.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C77 are supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 4E-G) with appropriate sample sizes (N=14-16). The ion selectivity experiments are well-controlled. The inference of marginal Ca2+ permeability from the negative ΔErev shift and remaining current is reasonable. The conclusion of a distinct channel is well-supported by the combined data.

results.result: flr-1 mutants (ut11, syb3521, and RNAi) show high DMP variability with very short and long cycles, missed EMCs, and weak pBocs; acd-3/del-5 double mutants phenocopy flr-1 defects, while single mutants show no phenotype, suggesting the three genes function together redundantly.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C87 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 5A-E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), citations to previous studies, and genetic interaction experiments. The phenocopy of flr-1 by acd-3/del-5 double mutants and lack of additional effect with flr-1(RNAi) provide strong evidence for a heteromeric complex. The redundancy of acd-3 and del-5 is well-supported by the lack of single mutant phenotypes.

results.result: The defects in acd-3/del-5 double mutants are rescued by expression of acd-3::mKate2 or mKate2::del-5 fusions, and intestine-specific expression of either acd-3 or del-5 rescues all defects, supporting the intestine as the site of function.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C93 are supported by rescue experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Table 1) and citations to previous studies. The rescue by fluorescent fusions confirms their functionality and validates the localization data. The intestine-specific rescue provides strong evidence for the site of action. Statistical tests are appropriate (Mann-Whitney U, Fisher exact test).

results.result: flr-1 and acd-3/del-5 mutations likely interfere with the intestinal Ca2+ wave; flr-1(syb3521) completely disrupts Ca2+ oscillation rhythmicity with significantly decreased basal and maximal Ca2+ concentrations, indicating the FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 channel plays a major role in controlling intestinal Ca2+ transients.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C100 are supported by citations to previous studies (C94-C95), phenotypic similarities (C96), and Ca2+ imaging data (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1-3). The complete disruption of Ca2+ rhythmicity in flr-1 mutants provides strong evidence for the channel's role upstream of or as part of the Ca2+ oscillator. Sample sizes are adequate (N=10-15).

results.result: flr-1(RNAi) impacts both intracellular and pseudocoelomic pH; basal pH is unaffected, but acidification accompanying pBoc is attenuated in both compartments, with evidence of shorter periodicity oscillations, demonstrating the FLR-1 channel controls proton release and pseudocoelomic pH.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C107 are supported by pH imaging data (Figure 7) with appropriate sample sizes (N=6). The use of ratiometric pH indicators (pHluorin and EC-sensor) is appropriate. The observation that basal pH is unaffected while dynamic acidification is attenuated is consistent with the proposed role. Statistical tests (unpaired t-tests) are appropriate.

results.result: flr-1 and acd-3/del-5 mutants show severe developmental delay (3x longer to adulthood), reduced body size, and caloric restriction-like appearance, while single acd-5, acd-3, and del-5 mutants show wild-type or slightly delayed development and normal size.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C118 are supported by citations to previous studies (C108-C109), visual observations (C110-C111, Figure 8—figure supplement 1), and quantitative measurements of developmental timing and body size (Figure 8A-C). Sample sizes are adequate (N=12-115). Statistical tests (Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's post hoc) are appropriate. The phenotypes are consistent with a role in development and growth.

results.result: flr-1 and acd-3/del-5 mutants show reduced intestinal fat accumulation (Oil-Red O staining), demonstrating aberrant fat metabolism consistent with reduced growth and body size, underlining the importance of proper DMP regulation by the FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 channel.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C127 are supported by citations to previous studies (C119-C123) and Oil-Red O staining data (Figure 8D). The authors appropriately note that Oil-Red O is qualitative rather than quantitative. The correlation between fat metabolism defects, growth defects, and DMP disruption is consistent with the proposed model. The link to nutrient uptake via proton gradients is well-established in the literature.

results.result: Two acid-sensitive DEG/ENaC channels with distinct functions exist: ACD-5 on the luminal membrane maintains acidic luminal pH and subtly influences DMP/Ca2+ oscillations; FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 on the basolateral membrane is essential for DMP timing and execution with consequences for fat metabolism and growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C133 are summary conclusions supported by the combined evidence from electrophysiology, localization, genetic analysis, Ca2+ imaging, pH imaging, and metabolic phenotyping presented throughout the manuscript. The distinct properties, localizations, and functional roles of the two channels are well-established by the data.

results.result: ACD-5 and FLR-1-containing channels exhibit very different pH dependence and kinetics; ACD-5 is fully open at pH 6 and closed at pH 4, while FLR-1 heteromers form a proton-inhibited cation leak channel similar to ACD-1, TadNaC6, and ASIC5; neither desensitizes, contrasting with mammalian ASICs.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C140 are supported by electrophysiological data (Figures 1, 4) and citations to previous studies. The comparison to other channels is appropriate. The lack of desensitization is directly observed in the recordings. The inference about ACD-5 activation ensuring return to pH~4 is reasonable given its role in maintaining luminal pH. The prediction that FLR-1 is constitutively open at pH 7.35 is well-supported by the pH dependence data and known pseudocoelomic pH.

results.result: All four intestinal DEG/ENaC subunits influence the DMP with dramatically different degrees; intestinal IP3-dependent Ca2+ signaling acts as the master oscillator; acd-5 mutant data supports Ca2+ oscillator dominance; ACD-5 acts downstream of the proton wave timing; there is a functional link between ACD-5 and VHA-6; the Ca2+ oscillator is upstream of and largely independent of lumen pH.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C154 are supported by the combined genetic, behavioral, and imaging data, along with citations to previous studies. The epistasis analysis, phenotypic comparisons, and genetic interactions provide strong evidence for the proposed relationships. The observation that Ca2+ oscillations and DMP rhythmicity are only subtly affected in acd-5 mutants despite dramatic pH disruption strongly supports the dominance of the Ca2+ oscillator.

results.result: flr-1 deficient animals exhibit dramatic DMP dysregulation with very long and short cycles; acd-3 and del-5 act redundantly in a heteromer with FLR-1; acd-3/del-5 double mutants phenocopy flr-1 loss of function; the severity is reminiscent of Ca2+ signaling disruption; flr-1(syb3521) completely disrupts Ca2+ transient rhythmicity, indicating the FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 channel is upstream of the Ca2+ oscillator, perhaps forming part of the master oscillator.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C163 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 5), Ca2+ imaging data (Figure 6), and citations to previous studies. The phenotypic similarities to itr-1 and unc-43 mutants support the link to Ca2+ signaling. The complete disruption of Ca2+ rhythmicity in flr-1 mutants provides strong evidence for an upstream role. The speculation about forming part of the master oscillator (C162) is appropriately qualified as tentative.

results.result: flr-1 and acd-3/del-5 mutants exhibit very short cycles ('echos') and missed/weak muscle contractions, linking phenotypes to disturbed Ca2+ signaling; shorter cycles indicate a role for calmodulin, CaMK II, and FLR-1 in retarding a shorter timescale oscillator; cycle variability represents loss of synchronicity between semi-independent oscillators; a constitutively open channel is consistent with maintaining cellular excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C171 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 5E), citations to previous studies, and the observed phenotypic similarities to unc-43 and cmd-1 mutants. The interpretations about oscillator interactions (C166-C167) and channel function (C168-C169) are reasonable inferences from the data, though appropriately speculative. The temporal relationship between Ca2+ and pseudocoelomic pH (C171) is supported by citation.

results.result: PBO-1 localizes to both membranes with distinct roles; ACD-3 and DEL-5 basolateral localization supports previous FLR-1 evidence; basolateral localization fits the pH dependence; an important remaining question is how FLR-1 influences Ca2+ and calmodulin signaling; the local nature of signaling events may explain why ACD-5 and FLR-1 have distinct effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C177 are supported by citations (C172), localization data (C173, Figure 4A-B), and logical inference (C174). The acknowledgment of remaining questions (C175-C176) is appropriate. The speculation about local signaling (C177) is reasonable but appropriately qualified as speculative.

results.result: Two acid-sensing DEG/ENaC channels play different roles in pH-Ca2+ interplay; ACD-5 maintains acidic lumen pH with subtle Ca2+ impact; FLR-1/ACD-3/DEL-5 is the essential link between pseudocoelomic pH and Ca2+; DEG/ENaCs are conserved and medically relevant; the data provide insight into channel properties and physiological roles; better understanding will help elucidate roles in other contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C185 are summary conclusions and broader implications supported by the entire body of work presented. The statements about conservation and medical relevance (C181-C182) are based on general knowledge. The significance statements (C183-C185) are appropriate given the comprehensive characterization of two distinct acid-sensing channels with different properties and roles.
